Work Products are used to describe tangible inputs or outputs that have the potential for reuse. They are intended to represent unique types of significant information. Work products do not have to equate to an individual document, but can be models, presentations, set of related documents, or even a set of values stored in a tool. Likewise, a single document may contain multiple work products. The same definition of a work product may be used to capture the same type of information across different areas and can be developed in an iterative fashion, with a work product being both the input and output of a given task as it is refined through the development lifecycle.
Deliverables describe how a set of work products are assembled and packaged for delivery and sign off to either an internal or external party. Deliverables are intended to present a starting point for the typical items that would be called out in a statement of work for a particular type of project. Deliverables are expressed based on a particular state at a given point in time and are expected to have an explicit set of completion criteria with any later refinements resulting in a new deliverable definition. Because they exist at a point intime they are not used as the primary inputs and outputs within a work breakdown structure but are limited to being output from the tasks related to preparing for delivery and then input to those related to review and sign-off.
Outcomes are used to describe intangible results that are achieved via the completion of a task or may also describe significant state changes that do not represent harvestable assets. Outcomes are defined less formally than other work products and may seem more general since they do not have templates or examples associated with them and often rely on their producing task for additional details or context.
